## Summary

P1 from the human, 2026-10-20 16:55Z: the Neovim workbench takes many minutes to start and slows the whole Mac while it loads. The explorer shows "loading the items…" for more than 5 minutes. The header says "no coordinator" and "sessions 0" while the hub is connected and holds the Coordinator and six sessions. The human: «запуск должен быть быстрым и если надо иметь ленивую подгрузку, но не так что десятками минут ждать», «весь мак жестко тормозит пока воркбенч грузится».

## Goal

The Neovim workbench starts fast: the explorer, the header's Coordinator and the session count appear within seconds on a large tracker, and loading never stalls the Mac.

## Notes

These are cland-impl's measurements at 16:57–17:00Z on the live project (1,005 items):
- Neovim re-polls `hub.status`, `task.list`, `topic.history(200)`, `events.list(200)`, `session.list`, `artifact.list`, `rule.list` and `account.list` about every 30 s, in a loop that never settles.
- `task.list` carries full bodies: 1,830,013 bytes.
- The `nvim --embed` process sits at about 58 % CPU and its RSS grows past 1.6 GB.
- Materialising each poll swings the hub between 80 MB and 912 MB RSS at 100 % CPU, and its `hub.status` answers take 1.4–2.7 s.
- `.cland/tasks` holds 6,029 files, of which 5,026 are `.conflict` captures. Almost every tracker write adds another, including plain `task create` and `task edit`. That churn keeps Spotlight and iCloud indexers busy.

The epic takes priority over every other v0.2 launch and over E-412 stage 2.

## Definition of done

- [ ] C1. On a copy of the live tracker (about 1,000 items), the Neovim workbench shows the open items, the sessions and the Coordinator within 3 s of the hub connection, measured on the human's Mac and recorded as local evidence.
  - verified: qa-676 [qa] · run qa-2026-10-22-1 · 2026-10-21T23:01:21.560Z · commit 5c9f87bad4c7434ca3048287e294d1fc981b7482
- [ ] C2. With the workbench idle for 10 minutes, no full re-read of the item list or any other whole-state list happens, and the hub's CPU stays near idle (local evidence).
  - verified: qa-676 [qa] · run qa-2026-10-22-1 · 2026-10-21T23:01:21.560Z · commit 5c9f87bad4c7434ca3048287e294d1fc981b7482
- [ ] C3. A Neovim smoke test with a 1,000-item fixture tracker fails when startup exceeds its budget or when the explorer's first payload exceeds its byte budget.
  - verified: qa-676 [qa] · run qa-2026-10-22-1 · 2026-10-21T23:01:21.560Z · commit 5c9f87bad4c7434ca3048287e294d1fc981b7482
- [ ] C4. Tracker writes from the hub and the CLI create no `.conflict` capture unless a real concurrent edit happened, and old captures are pruned by a documented retention rule (with T-452).
  - verified: qa-676 [qa] · run qa-2026-10-22-1 · 2026-10-21T23:01:21.560Z · commit 5c9f87bad4c7434ca3048287e294d1fc981b7482

items.name: M-1-cland-v0-the-way-to-a-buildable-spec.md
items.text:
---
id: M-1
kind: map
title: "cland v0: the way to a buildable spec"
state: closed
labels:
  - wayfinder:map
assignee: null
parent: null
blocked_by: []
topic: null
branch: null
created: 2026-10-07T14:51:04Z
updated: 2026-10-08T13:17:15.582Z
github:
  repo: Kealman/cland-v0
  number: 1
  url: https://github.com/Kealman/cland-v0/issues/1
---

## Destination

A spec for cland v0, the terminal IDE for agent harnesses: the architecture decisions recorded as ADRs in this repo (engine, hub, topic model, task tracking, git strategy, artifacts, harness adapters, roles, review and QA process), a glossary, and a first-slice cut, ready to be broken into implementation tickets with `/to-tickets`. The map decides; building is a separate effort.

## Notes

Domain: see `GLOSSARY.md` (Harness, Session, Role, Coordinator, Hub, Topic, Artifact). Product name: cland.

Settled at charting (not tickets):

- Single-user tool, one cland instance per project, started from the repo root.
- Neovim as the engine is the leading candidate, validated by a prototype ticket before an ADR locks it.
- v0 harnesses: Claude Code, Codex (as a full interactive harness, not only `exec`), OpenCode; one adapter layer designed for more.
- Role is first-class: assigned to a session, independent of harness and model, movable mid-project.
- The process layer (Matt Pocock's skills, adapted) is part of cland.
- The reusable core of the BCAS driver hub (`/Users/evgeniyivanov/Projects/BratvaInc/bcas/tooling/driver-hub`) is the starting codebase for the hub, not only inspiration.
- cland must know each session's state (idle, busy, waiting for the human, waiting for approval) from a reliable source, not from the model's self-report.

Working rules for every session on this map:

1. Everything written to this repo or the tracker is in English. The conversation with the human is in Russian.
2. The coordinator thinks, coordinates and decides; sub-agents on opus/sonnet do all direct work, at high effort by default (lower when the task allows).
3. Review (gpt 6.1 sol) and QA (gpt 6 astra, computer use) go through `/codex:rescue` only. If it fails, fix the chain or report to the human; never do their work for them.
4. Grilling tickets: call the Skill tool for `grilling` and `domain-modeling`. Prototype tickets: `prototype`. Research tickets: `research`; findings live in `docs/research/<name>.md` on a throwaway branch `research/<name>` (pushed, never merged, no PR).
5. ADRs in `docs/adr/`, glossary in `GLOSSARY.md`, both in this repo on `main`.

## Decisions so far

- [Research: what in the BCAS driver hub is reusable for cland](https://github.com/Kealman/cland-v0/issues/2): one Node service + per-session MCP spoke over WebSocket + SQLite; reuse the spoke, protocol, hub-client, Codex App Server supervisor, store-and-forward and HumanSide port nearly as-is; re-implement asks, roles, slots and add session state (absent in BCAS); drop Discord, the evidence CLI and boards. Findings: `docs/research/bcas-hub.md` on branch `research/bcas-hub`.
- [Research: harness integration surfaces for Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode](https://github.com/Kealman/cland-v0/issues/3): all three expose session state that does not come from the model, in different shapes: Codex app-server `thread/status/changed` (`idle` / `active` plus `waitingOnApproval` / `waitingOnUserInput`), OpenCode SSE events plus `GET /api/session/active` (no "waiting" status), Claude Code hooks and mods in-session plus polled `claude agents --json` (`busy` / `waiting` / `idle` with `waitingFor`). Codex and OpenCode run sessions on a local server the host joins as a client; Claude Code has no server but `--bg` plus `attach`. The host can answer approvals and inject messages in all three; channels remain a research preview. Same `SKILL.md` format, different directories; `AGENTS.md` / `CLAUDE.md` handling differs per harness. Versions: Claude Code 2.1.292, Codex 0.160.0, OpenCode 2.0.24. Findings: `docs/research/harness-surfaces.md` on branch `research/harness-surfaces`.
- [Research: what the latest Neovim release offers as the cland engine](https://github.com/Kealman/cland-v0/issues/4): stable is 0.12.5 (2026-08-23), 0.13 due 2026-10-15; Lua primitives cover a chat panel (splits, floats, extmarks, prompt buffers) and processes (`vim.system`, `vim.uv`, msgpack-RPC both ways); `NVIM_APPNAME` isolates a standalone build; the built-in terminal (libvterm) is the weak spot: limited key fidelity (Shift+Enter), pastes drop TABs by default, no images, terminals die with the Neovim process, open bugs with floats over terminals; no WebSocket client and no SQLite module in Lua. Findings: `docs/research/neovim-engine.md` on branch `research/neovim-engine`.
- [Research: self-hostable git engines for an agents-only territory](https://github.com/Kealman/cland-v0/issues/5): no agent-first self-hostable git engine exists; the realistic territories are plain Git plus a cland-owned review layer, a local Gitea / Forgejo forge (Gitea 28.1 verified end to end on macOS arm64: bot accounts, REST-driven PRs, reviews, required approvals, auto-merge), or Radicle (mid-transition, security fix pending in 2.0); a reviewer must be a separate identity everywhere; hundreds of open PRs on one base branch slow every merge; GitHub alone is insufficient on a personal account (no merge queue, no counted self-approval); the release squash to GitHub is always a separate, cland-owned step. Findings: `docs/research/git-engines.md` on branch `research/git-engines`.
- [Task: smoke-test codex:rescue with gpt 6.1 sol and gpt 6 astra](https://github.com/Kealman/cland-v0/issues/6): the chain works through `/codex:rescue --model gpt-6.1-sol` (review) and `--model gpt-6-astra` (QA), verified by the Codex rollouts (both at reasoning effort high from `~/.codex/config.toml`); astra's computer use is a browser-surface JS REPL (`mcp__cua_repl.js`) and refuses to drive the terminal app ("Computer Use is not allowed to use the app 'com.mitchellh.ghostty'"), so terminal QA needs another surface; shell access works.
- [Topic model: lifecycle, statuses, ownership and the single agent context](https://github.com/Kealman/cland-v0/issues/7): one flat list per project with two standing topics (General, Agents); a topic has a title, a status (open / waiting for human / waiting for agent / closed, set by message direction plus explicit `ask` and `resolve`) and at most one binding to a unit of work, with at most one topic per unit of work; messages address the Coordinator role by default and `@role` / `@session` pull others in; Ask is a message kind with options and a free answer; agents have no current topic, every delivery carries the topic id and history is pulled on demand; no ADR.
- [Role model: which roles exist, what a role carries, and how a role moves between sessions](https://github.com/Kealman/cland-v0/issues/10): four roles (Coordinator exclusive, Implementer, Reviewer, QA) plus roleless sessions off the hub; a role carries a clause, a skill list, hub-enforced permissions and launch defaults (Coordinator Claude Code/Fable, Implementer OpenCode/free model, Reviewer Codex/sol, QA Codex/astra); the clause is delivered by hub events, never by harness-native instruction pins; role-bound state lives in the hub and a handover note moves the role, never the transcript; only the Coordinator asks the human; ADR 0001.
- [Task tracking: own tracker, GitHub wrapper or hybrid](https://github.com/Kealman/cland-v0/issues/8): cland's own tracker is the source of truth, GitHub sync stays in the fog; one entity Item with kinds (epic, spec, task, question, map), GitHub-issue-shaped fields plus topic and branch links, claims, verdicts and cost; one Markdown file per item with YAML frontmatter, committed in the repo, written through the hub which keeps a SQLite index and the live state; comments and structured verdicts in the file; CLI `cland task` plus hub tools, so the skills work in their "other" tracker mode; sequential ids `T-123`; no auto-commits; ADR 0002.
- [Hub boundaries: what the hub owns, its transport, persistence and the nvim bridge](https://github.com/Kealman/cland-v0/issues/13): a per-project daemon independent of the UI, extracted from the BCAS core (Node/TS, SQLite, WebSocket spoke), owning the session registry, routing with store-and-forward and three delivery stages (queued, delivered, injected), topics and asks, role state and permission enforcement, the tracker index and live claims, and the journal; adapters launch and supervise harness processes and the UI attaches to them; the Neovim UI speaks the same frames as JSON lines over a Unix socket; normalised session state from reliable signals; secret file and database in the project's cland folder, never committed; ADR 0003.
- [Harness adapter contract: what every adapter must provide](https://github.com/Kealman/cland-v0/issues/12): mandatory `spawn`, `attach_command`, `inject` (confirming the injected stage), a normalised state stream, `stop` and `resume`; optional `history`, `usage`, `set_model` and approval relay, declared as capabilities with per-signal reliability; the v0 mapping is fixed for Codex (app-server plus `resume --remote`), OpenCode (server plus TUI client, heuristic waiting) and Claude Code (`--bg` plus `attach`, mod-based inject, hooks for state); adapters are hub modules with harness processes in the hub's process table; failures surface as stage and state and never block the queue; approvals stay in the harness TUI in v0; no ADR.
- [Git strategy: an agents-only territory and what flows to GitHub](https://github.com/Kealman/cland-v0/issues/14): plain git with a cland-owned layer, no forge; the project's `origin` is a local bare repository (the territory) inside the cland folder and GitHub is the remote `github` touched only by releases; `main` mirrors GitHub, `dev` integrates, task branches `t/T-123-slug` in cland-made worktrees land on `dev` as one squash commit each through `cland merge`, which requires clear review and (where marked) QA verdicts from the right roles; `cland release` fast-forwards `main` to `dev`, tags `vX.Y.Z` with notes from item titles and pushes to GitHub; `cland init` re-points an existing project reversibly; ADR 0004.
- [Research: QA of a terminal IDE with gpt 6 astra computer use](https://github.com/Kealman/cland-v0/issues/16): astra cannot drive a native terminal through `/codex:rescue` and no setting changes that (terminals are blocked in the signed Computer Use helper, and approvals are auto-declined inside rescue runs); three verified lanes remain: a headless Neovim driven by `nvim_input` with the grid read by `screenstring()` (the default, no grant needed), tmux with `capture-pane` (needs `network_access = true` in the Codex sandbox), and a ttyd web terminal in Chrome on a pre-allowed origin; the sandbox blocks Unix sockets while network is off, so sandboxed QA uses a stdio link to the hub (ADR 0003 addendum); long runs go `--background`; verdicts as structured item comments. Findings: `docs/research/qa-astra.md` on branch `research/qa-astra`.
- [Artifact model: where artifacts live, their lifecycle, and how agents show things to the human](https://github.com/Kealman/cland-v0/issues/9): artifacts are plain files in the project's cland folder with a hub index, not committed unless promoted into the repo; ids `A-123`; kinds prompt, note, page, diagram, file; Markdown and Mermaid render in Neovim, HTML and images open in the browser; long prompts are drafted as `prompt` artifacts and sent or attached; agents share through `artifact.create`, which posts into the topic; statuses draft, sent, shared, archived with time-based cleanup; bound to topics, never to sessions; no ADR.
- [Process layer: what cland provisions into a project](https://github.com/Kealman/cland-v0/issues/17): skills in `.agents/skills` with `.claude/skills` symlinked, `docs/agents/*`, `AGENTS.md` only (never `CLAUDE.md`; an `@AGENTS.md` import if one exists), the roles config, Claude Code hooks and the cland mod, all marked "managed by cland" and refreshed by `cland init` / `cland update` without touching anything else; the Matt Pocock skills vendored with cland's patches plus `qa`, `release`, `merge` and `handover`; only secret-free files are committed; `cland doctor` checks the toolchain; the cland folder is `.cland/` with `tasks/`, `roles.toml` and `config.toml` committed and `artifacts/`, `worktrees/`, `territory.git/`, `hub.db`, `hub.json`, `secret`, `journal.jsonl` ignored; no ADR.
- [Prototype: Neovim as host versus Neovim as embedded component](https://github.com/Kealman/cland-v0/issues/11): Neovim is the host; the prototype on branch `prototype/nvim-host` passed all three showstoppers and the human's checklist with the real harnesses; the terminal's failures (Shift+Enter, pasted TABs, scrollback default, terminals dying on `:restart`, alternate-screen history, UI updates waiting on pending input) are mitigated in cland's configuration and by owning sessions outside Neovim; embedding Neovim in an own host is rejected; ADR 0005.
- [Prototype: the chat screen with topics](https://github.com/Kealman/cland-v0/issues/15): the main screen is one shell with toggleable panels, accepted for v0: a centre view (thread, board, item, session, Agents log, inbox full width), a left items panel with filters including the wayfinder map, one right panel (inbox, sessions or topics), one floating picker, the three motions `gi` / `gt` / `gs`, and stage presets as examples rather than modes; design canvas and branch `prototype/workbench`; the per-item change tour is parked in the fog.
- [First usable slice: what goes into the first daily-driver build](https://github.com/Kealman/cland-v0/issues/18): slice 1 is the daily driver (shell, hub, adapters, roles, tracker, process layer, review and QA through the roles) in six tracer bullets, done when the human runs a real cland task inside cland; slice 2 adds the git territory, artifacts, the QA lane infrastructure and UI additions; tracker bootstrap on GitHub Issues; repository layout `hub/`, `nvim/`, `skills/`, `docs/`; recorded in `docs/spec/v0.md`.

## Not yet specified

- Engine: distribution format of the standalone build; keymap scheme.
- Sessions: restoring sessions after an IDE restart; binding a session to a git worktree.
- Chat: message rendering (Markdown, code, artifacts inline); searching history.
- Task tracking: the entity model (task, epic, milestone, question); binding topics to tasks; plugging the skills into an own tracker through their "other" tracker mode.
- Git: a worktree per session; branch integration policy; the release flow into GitHub.
- Artifacts: rendering HTML and diagrams from a terminal (browser hand-off, terminal graphics protocols); versioning.
- Hub: security of local connections; an ingress for automation; asks with options and approval relays rendered in the IDE.
- Review and QA as a cland feature: the coordinator running review (sol) and QA (astra) rounds as harness sessions, distinct from the process used to build cland itself.
- Ideas to revisit: a sessions board (role, harness, model, state and current task of every session at a glance); cost and usage per session, role and model; crew presets (launch a standard set of sessions for a task type in one command); a unified event journal across sessions for retrospectives and recovery.
- Change tour per item: look at what an item changed as the project is now, navigated by file structure, with new or changed places marked in the gutter rather than a red and green diff; spawn a session on the item's worktree or context to ask for a diagram or an explanation.

## Out of scope

- Multi-user mode, accounts and permissions.
- A GUI outside the terminal.
- Cloud hosting of cland.
- Remote access (from a phone or another machine) for v0.

## Comments

### Kealman · 2026-10-08T11:33:59Z

<!-- github-comment: 6058950178 -->

## Map complete (2026-10-08)

All 17 tickets are closed. The destination is reached: `docs/spec/v0.md` on `main` (225f725), with ADR 0001 to 0005 in `docs/adr/` and `GLOSSARY.md`. Research findings stay on the `research/*` branches, prototypes on the `prototype/*` branches, none merged.

id: Q-10

title: "Role model: which roles exist, what a role carries, and how a role moves
  between sessions"
state: closed

assignee: Kealman
parent: M-1

created: 2026-10-07T14:52:15Z

github:
  repo: Kealman/cland-v0
  number: 10
  url: https://github.com/Kealman/cland-v0/issues/10
---

## Question

Which roles exist in v0 (Coordinator, Reviewer, QA, Implementer, others?), what does a role carry (instructions, skills, permissions, default harness and model), and how does a role move between sessions mid-project?

The central question is continuity: when the Coordinator role moves from one session to another (for example from Claude Code on Fable to a cheaper model in OpenCode for a simple stretch), how are topic history, current tasks and unresolved decisions handed over?

Decide whether roles are exclusive, how the human assigns and revokes them, and what the hub enforces. Produce glossary entries and an ADR if the choice is hard to reverse.

Context: BCAS had driver / qa / reviewer / worker roles in JSON with a clause each, and an exclusive coordinator seat with manual handover (`/role set`). See branch `research/bcas-hub`.

## Comments

### Kealman · 2026-10-07T16:19:46Z

<!-- github-comment: 6042041053 -->

## Facts from research that bear on this decision

From `docs/research/harness-surfaces.md` (branch `research/harness-surfaces`) and `docs/research/bcas-hub.md` (branch `research/bcas-hub`):

- **Delivering a role's instructions differs per harness.** Claude Code reads `CLAUDE.md` (and `AGENTS.md` only when no `CLAUDE.md` exists); Codex reads `AGENTS.md` (and `CLAUDE.md` only via a fallback setting); OpenCode reads `AGENTS.md` only. Pinning Codex instructions with `-c developer_instructions` (the BCAS reviewer pin) drops the TUI into embedded mode with no external surface, so a role clause for Codex needs another path (app-server config at thread start, `AGENTS.md`, or a hub event).
- **Skills reach all three** through the same `SKILL.md` format but different directories (`.claude/skills`, `.agents/skills`, both for OpenCode); the symlink layout in this repo reaches all three.
- **Handover surfaces.** Claude Code: `--resume` and transcripts under `~/.claude/projects`; Codex: `thread/resume` on the app-server, `thread/inject_items` for an empty thread; OpenCode: sessions live on the service and are listed over its API. BCAS handed the coordinator seat over with a manual `/role set` plus a note; it kept role clauses as hub events because MCP instructions are fixed at connect.

### Kealman · 2026-10-07T17:04:14Z

<!-- github-comment: 6042750491 -->

## Resolution

Decided on 2026-10-07 in a grilling session with the human. `GLOSSARY.md` (1d821e4) carries the terms; ADR 0001, `docs/adr/0001-roles-are-hub-held-state.md`, records the architectural choice and the rejected options.

**Roles in v0.** Coordinator, Implementer, Reviewer, QA. Sessions without a role are allowed: they are the human's own terminals and do not connect to the hub. Research is not a role; the Coordinator's sub-agents do it. A session has at most one role. Coordinator is exclusive (one holder or vacant); the other roles may have many holders.

**What a role carries.** (a) A role clause (instruction text); (b) a skill list; (c) hub permissions the hub enforces; (d) launch defaults: harness, model, effort. Definitions live in project-level config that cland provisions with defaults and the human edits; the file layout is decided with the state layout and the process layer (#17).

**Launch defaults (initial values, editable at any time).** Coordinator = Claude Code, Fable, effort max. Implementer = OpenCode with a free model (to be picked), so that all three harnesses are exercised from day one. Reviewer = Codex, gpt-6.1-sol, high. QA = Codex, gpt-6-astra, high. A session may switch model mid-role where the harness allows; defaults apply only at launch; the hub shows the current model as reported by the adapter.

**Clause delivery.** Uniformly through the hub, as an event at assignment and on every reconnect. Harness-native instruction files (`CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`) carry only the generic "you are a cland session" part. No `-c developer_instructions` for Codex: it drops the TUI into embedded mode with no external surface.

**Hub permissions by role.**

- Coordinator: `send` to anyone; `ask` the human; create topics; claim tasks and assign tasks to others; request launching sessions with roles; hand over its own role; `resolve`.
- Implementer: `send` (to the Coordinator and to mentioned parties); create topics bound to its own task; claim its own task. No `ask`, no role operations.
- Reviewer and QA: `send` (verdicts as plain messages to the Coordinator), `history`, `who`. No claims, no `ask`, no topics.
- No role: not connected to the hub.

Everything else, such as closing topics, the human does through the UI. Implementer, Reviewer and QA ask the Coordinator with plain messages (visible in the Agents topic); only the Coordinator asks the human, through Ask.

**Assignment and handover.** The human assigns and revokes roles, in the UI or at launch. The Coordinator may request sessions with roles and may hand its own role to another session with a handover note. No other role assigns roles. The hub enforces Coordinator exclusivity. A dead session's role becomes vacant; no auto-reassignment; a vacant Coordinator shows a "no coordinator" warning. A session that reconnects under the same name gets its role and clause back. A holder whose role is revoked mid-work receives a "role revoked" event and must stop acting in that role.

**Context handover.** Role-bound state lives in the hub, not in the session. The next holder receives: (1) the clause; (2) the handover note, mandatory when the holder hands over and optional when the human reassigns, a Markdown template with four sections: goals now, work in flight, open decisions, waiting on; it is stored in the hub as part of the role's state, delivered as an event and recorded in the Agents topic; (3) on demand from the hub: topics `waiting for agent`, open asks, the role's task claims, topic history. The old session's transcript never moves. The old session lives on without a role, or as an Implementer.

**Identity.** A session has a name (`[a-z0-9-]`, chosen by the human or generated), shown everywhere with its role, for example `reviewer-1 [Reviewer]`. Roles move between names; names do not change.

**Not decided here.** Exact skill lists per role and how skills reach each harness (#17); the adapter and hub mechanics of event delivery (#12, #13); crew presets (fog).

### Kealman · 2026-10-08T08:15:02Z

<!-- github-comment: 6055699849 -->

## Addendum (2026-10-07): item operations and verdicts by role

Confirmed by the human while the v0 spec was being written, resolving a gap between #10, #8 and #14:

- **Verdicts.** Reviewer and QA sessions write their verdicts as structured comments on the item through the hub (`task.comment`, restricted to verdict comments), as #8 and the merge gate in #14 require. Their permission set is therefore `send`, `history`, `who` and verdict comments on items.
- **Item operations.** The Coordinator and the human create items (the Coordinator through `to-tickets`); the Coordinator edits and closes items; an Implementer may comment on and claim its own item; Reviewer and QA write only verdicts.
- **Review and QA in slice 1.** Both roles work for real from slice 1: the Coordinator sends a review or QA request through the hub to a Codex session holding the role, which writes the verdict on the item; `/codex:rescue` stays the fallback. Only the QA lane infrastructure (the Lua QA API, brief format, the `qa` skill, the hub's stdio transport) is slice 2.

## Summary

It hit T-1341's rule 6 run 09c84a9b (A-12503, Linux) and older logs (A-1151, A-1544, A-1551). It passed 5/5 alone. The test advances its injected clock by 150 ms once, right after `killDaemon`. items.name: E-386-test-speed-quick-wins.md
items.text:
---
id: E-386
kind: epic
title: "Test speed: quick wins"
state: closed
criterion_seq: 9
labels:
  - epic
  - v0.1.2
  - ready-for-agent
assignee: null
parent: R-228
blocked_by: []
topic: topic-272
branch: null
created: 2026-10-14T12:28:09.133Z
updated: 2026-10-15T07:45:20.712Z
closed: 2026-10-15T07:45:20.712Z
---

## Goal

A task's verification stops costing a full suite, and the full suite costs less machine time per test, without any test losing what it proves. Today a task waits about 39 minutes for its verification: 24 minutes of queue and 15 minutes of run. 37 of the last 40 task merges ran the full suite. 81% of test-time sits in tests that spawn a real hub, driven by about 63,000 process spawns per run, of which 29,203 are `ps`, `lsof` and `pgrep` calls. These five changes are the cheap half of the research's recommended epic: no fixture redesign, no assertion changed in meaning. They cut about 4–5 minutes from a local full run, take Neovim-only tasks from about 15 minutes to about 2, and stop the suite growing by about 2.4 minutes a day without anyone noticing (Q-384, `docs/research/test-speed.md`).

## Contents

- **Selection hygiene (§3.3(a), §3.10 "D29 hygiene").** The docs, the clauses and the QA skill stop prescribing `cland verify all` for task runs, as D29 says. `chooseSuiteMode` widens from positive allowlists to package rules. Replayed on the last 40 merges, those rules turn full 37 / hub-only 2 / Neovim-only 1 into about full 22 / hub-only 13 / Neovim-only 5.
- **The timing diet (§3.9).** Fast fake-harness defaults, with an explicit opt-in for tests that need a slow turn to stage a race. Env control over the production schedules that tests wait out in real time: the 30-second Claude agents schedule, the executor lifetime, run timeout and sweep, and accounts polling. Event waits replace fixed sleeps of 0.5 s or more where the sleep waits for something to happen.
- **The duration manifest and the slow-test budget (§3.7).** `hub/test/durations.json` is generated from a green integrated log. A budget check fails a test over 5 s or a file over 60 s unless the manifest lists it with a reason. The suite report names the top regressions.
- **Lazy CLI subcommand imports (§3.10).** `hub/bin/cland.ts` loads only the subcommand it runs, with a module-count guard test. This applies to about 3,700 CLI processes per run and to every agent's own `cland` call.
- **The process-inspection diet (§3.5).** Fixture hubs skip the start-up orphan sweep unless the test opts in. Teardown kills from the recorded ownership table instead of scanning the machine. `processStarted` calls are coalesced. The census target is under 12,000 `ps` + `lsof` + `pgrep` spawns per run.

Not in this epic: the in-process hub fixture, coverage-based selection, droplet sharding and the worker re-measurement. Those are "Test speed: structural" in v0.1.3 (R-294), the research's #6 to #9. Also out: fixture snapshots of seeded `.cland` state (§3.2), running the Neovim phase alongside the hub phase (§3.10, the research's open question 7), and splitting `suite.test.ts` and `merge.test.ts`, which goes with the sharding ticket.

Choices where the research is silent:

- **Package rules.** `nvim-only` is any diff wholly under `nvim/**` except the protocol-side `nvim/lua/cland/hub.lua` and `state.lua`. `full` is a diff that touches both packages, or touches one of these: the protocol, the adapter contract, the crew and role CLI, the package, lockfile and tsconfig files, the suite runner and selection modules, or any hub file that `nvim/test/**` imports directly (today `hub/test/harness.ts`, `hub/test/process-cleanup.ts`, `hub/src/protocol.ts`, five tracker modules, `init/config.ts`, `hub/store.ts` and the two visibility modules). The import list is read from the source at selection time, not hard-coded. `hub-only` is everything else, docs, skills, `.agents/` and `.cland/tasks/` included. Integrated `dev`, empty diffs and fetch failures still run full.
- **Fast defaults.** Fake turns take 30 ms, adapter polls run every 50 ms and push trust is 100 ms. The Codex refuse window is 150 ms. A test that needs a slow turn passes `turnMs` (or the fake's existing "take your time" text) and says why in a comment. Tests that prove a default value (the 30-second schedule) prove it from the resolved setting the hub reports, and prove the behaviour at a short override. All timing control uses the existing `CLAND_*_MS` and `CLAND_TEST_*` environment pattern. Nothing adds an injected clock or any other new seam inside the hub.
- **Negative waits** ("nothing happens for N ms") are not event waits. Each one becomes a multiple of the interval it waits out, so it shrinks with the new defaults and still spans the same number of polls.
- **The budget** is 5 s per test and 60 s per file, judged on raw time in the run that executed the file. A test absent from the manifest and over budget fails the run with a `duration budget` line naming it. Allowlist entries carry a reason and the recorded median. The Coordinator refreshes the manifest from a green integrated log at each stage close. Times only fall during this epic, so a stale manifest never produces a false failure.
- **Fixture sweeps.** `startDaemon` sets `CLAND_TEST_SKIP_ORPHAN_SWEEP=1` by default, and the daemon skips the start-up sweep only when that variable is set. These tests opt back in by fixture option: `orphan-servers`, `orphan-sweep-lock`, `daemon`, `doctor*`, `system-processes`, `termination-ownership` and every test that asserts an `orphan-sweep-*` journal event. Production hubs never see the variable.
- **Teardown ownership.** A test's teardown signals only identities it recorded (pid with start time), verified by a targeted `ps -p`. The machine-wide `ps eww -ax` and `lsof -d cwd` scan stays in the runner's phase sweep and in the root-directory cleanup path. The coalescing of `processStarted` lives no longer than one operation, so pid reuse is still detected.

## Tracer-bullet order

1. **Selection that selects.** Widened package rules, plus docs, clauses and the QA skill aligned with D29. Demo: `cland verify` with no mode on a branch that changes only `nvim/lua/cland/explorer.lua` selects `nvim-only` and finishes in under 3 minutes. The 40-merge replay table shows the new split.
2. **The timing diet.** Fast fake defaults with explicit slow opt-ins, env control over the timer-bound tests, and event waits. Demo: the three slowest timer-bound tests (`executor-safety` "prepare, run, fallback, cancel…", `claude-code-adapter` "…default 30-second schedule…", `executor-safety` "…timed-out run…") each take under 5 s alone.
3. **Lazy CLI imports.** `cland --help` loads a handful of modules, and each subcommand loads only its own closure. Demo: the guard test prints the module counts per command, and `cland --help` takes under 50 ms on an idle machine.
4. **The inspection diet.** No sweep in fixture hubs unless asked, teardown from the ownership table, coalesced `processStarted`. Demo: a census compare against A-2021 shows `ps` + `lsof` + `pgrep` under 12,000.
5. **The budget.** `hub/test/durations.json` from the latest green integrated log, the budget check in the runner and the regressions in the suite report. Demo: a planted 6-second test in a scratch branch fails its run with a `duration budget` line, and the report lists the top regressions.

## Dogfooding

From the first merge on, the crew's task runs select by the wider rules, so most hub tasks skip the Neovim phase and Neovim tasks skip the hub phase. Every later stage of v0.1.2 waits less in the queue. The Coordinator relaunches the role sessions after the selection ticket merges, because clauses are fixed at launch. From the budget ticket on, the Coordinator refreshes `hub/test/durations.json` at each stage close of the release, and over-budget tests reach review with their reason.

## Constraints

- **Standing rules.** Every artifact, item, commit and doc is in English. Sub-agents never use the hub: the cland tools belong to the session that started them. Only `cland release` pushes to GitHub. Commit on the task branch `t/<id>-<slug>` in its worktree, push it to `origin`, the local territory, and reach `dev` only through `cland merge` and its verdict gate. Suites run through `cland verify`.
- **Frame-protocol-first tests stay meaningful.** Tests go through the hub's frame protocol first (a real hub, a real spoke, the CLI against a temporary project; `hub/test/harness.ts`) and the fake harnesses in `hub/test/fakes/` second, with the Neovim UI headless from the protocol's other side. Nothing here adds a seam inside the hub. Timing control uses the existing environment knobs. No test is deleted or weakened to save time. A change to an assertion keeps what it proves, and the reviewer checks this per changed assertion.
- **D25 review-first.** Request source review first. After a clear source verdict, `cland verify` runs at the exact reviewed head. A fix needs a new review before a new run.
- **D29.** Task runs verify only what the diff selects, never `cland verify all` unless the selection or the Coordinator asks. Full suites run as integrated `dev` runs per batch of about three merges, at every stage and epic close, and before release. D28 sends verification to droplets. Before/after measurements compare runs on the same executor and size.
- **The load rule.** Stress loops, repeated whole-file proofs and census runs are suite-weight. They start only when the verify queue has no holder and no waiter (T-204, incident of 2026-10-12 19:05Z). Single-file timings for criteria are taken on an idle machine and posted with the one-minute load.
- **Races exposed by faster fakes.** If a fast default exposes a race, it is a product defect: the Implementer reports it to `lead T-<n>` as a Bug with its size. Until the fix lands, the affected test may opt into the old timing with a comment naming the bug. A test never opts in silently.
- **ADRs.** 0003 (The hub is a per-project daemon): lifecycle proofs keep a real spawned daemon in this epic. 0002 (Tracker files are the source of truth): the duration manifest is a repository file, not hub state.
- **Risks.** Faster fakes can turn latent races into flakes, as load did in T-369 to T-383. Skipping fixture sweeps can hide a leak between tests, which the runner's phase sweep and the dedicated orphan tests still catch. A hub-only selection can miss a Neovim regression caused by an event-shape change, so D29's integrated batch run is the backstop. A budget judged on raw time can flap under load spikes, which an allowlist entry with a reason absorbs.
- **Order.** Inside v0.1.2 now, by the human's decision of 2026-10-14 12:15Z. It runs beside the release's other lanes. Its merges follow the batch-merge rule.

## Summary

The project's rules move out of one session's memory into a rulebook kept with the project, fed into every role's clause and brief, and delivered to running sessions when a rule changes. The Coordinator gets a heartbeat that wakes it with a digest of what looks stale, and a lane's next epic starts on the previous epic's last merge while that epic's demo runs on a droplet, so the crew never waits on a frozen `dev`.

## Goal

Every session of every harness reads the same project rules, a broken chain of events is noticed within the hour, and the crew never idles between epics. Today the rules the human stated during the work (which model for which role, one suite at a time, how briefs address roles, when to merge) live in the Coordinator's harness memory: another harness cannot read them, and nobody can see them whole (Q-378). The human kept an hourly check running outside the hub so that a review nobody requested or an ask nobody answered got noticed (Q-380). During v0.1.2 the crew went fully idle twice, from 13:50 to 14:22Z on 2026-10-13 and in shorter gaps before, because each lane waited for an integrated run, a hub restart and an epic demo before the next epic was cut, and twice the stand-in unlinked a lane-order edge by hand (T-335).

## Contents

- **§3.2 The rulebook.**
  - **The file.** `.cland/RULES.md` in the project: one rule per heading with an id a plain number, a scope (all roles or named roles), the date, the reason and a status (active, retired). AGENTS.md stays the hand-written static instructions, and the harness memories become caches of what the rulebook holds.
  - **How a rule is added.** `cland rule add` from the shell or the workbench, and a `rule.add` tool for sessions: the Coordinator records a rule when the human states one in a thread, instead of writing it into its private memory. A rule is edited and retired the same way.
  - **How it reaches sessions.** The hub puts the rules of a role into its clause at launch and into the brief, and delivers a new or changed rule to running sessions as a delivery (ADR 0007). The workbench shows the rulebook with each rule's origin.
  - **The seed.** One Aide task migrates the rules this project accumulated in the planning session's and the stand-in's memories: briefs address the role; no long foreground commands; one suite at a time; verdicts go to the lead; no routing around refusals; the batch-merge rule; verify the head before merging; check the verify queue before committing on `dev`.
- **§3.3 The heartbeat.**
  - **Interval per role** in `crew.toml`: `heartbeat = "1h"` for the Coordinator by default, off for the other roles unless set.
  - **The delivery** carries a digest the hub computes: what is in flight and what looks stale (items in review with no verdict requested, ready items not merged, sessions idle longer than `idle_minutes`, runs that never reported, asks nobody answered).
  - **When it fires.** A heartbeat starts a turn only when the session is idle; otherwise it folds into the next turn's digest (v0.1 §3.9 hygiene). It is never a needs-you, it shows in the events view, and the timer is an event kind under ADR 0007.
  - **The clause** of the Coordinator says what to check on a heartbeat, what to repair and when to escalate to the human.
- **§3.4 Lane flow.**
  - **The next epic starts on the last merge.** A lane's next epic may be cut (`to-tickets`, `plan-epic`) and its first stage launched as soon as the previous epic's last ticket merges. The previous epic's QA demo runs in parallel and still closes the epic and gates the release (D16). Merges of the next epic's tickets that touch the same surfaces wait for the demo's verdict, so that the verdict sits on the `dev` tip. The next epic's to-tickets and plan-epic are prepared while the previous epic's last stage is in review.
  - **`follows`, not `blocked_by`.** Lane order is a relation of its own, `follows`, so that nobody unlinks blocking edges by hand; `blocked_by` keeps meaning a real dependency.
  - **Demos off `dev`.** Epic demos run on a droplet (v0.1.2 §3.14), so that `dev` need not freeze for them.

Not in this epic: the rulebook and the heartbeat in the web workbench (v0.2); rules shared across projects (the rulebook is the project's own); any change to D16, under which a QA demo still closes an epic and gates the release.

Choices where the spec is silent:

- **The file's shape.** Each rule is a heading `## <n> <short title>`, then one line per field (`Scope: all` or `Scope: coordinator, implementer`; `Date:`; `Status: active` or `Status: retired <date>`; `Origin:`; `Reason:`), then the rule's text as a paragraph. Numbers count up in the file and are never reused, and a retired rule stays in it. The hub writes the file and re-reads it when it changes, as it does `roles.toml`, so a hand edit or a merge that changes it is read and delivered too; a file that does not parse is logged and the last good version stays in force. `cland init` writes an empty rulebook with a one-line header.
- **Rule ids beside item ids.** `R-` is also the release prefix, and any prefix with a number resolves an item (v0.1.2 §3.1). Outside the rulebook a rule is always written `rule <n>`: clauses, briefs, deliveries and the events view use that form, and the workbench resolves `rule <n>` to the rulebook while a bare `<n>` stays an item reference. Rule numbers are the rulebook's own, not the item counter's.
- **The commands and tools.** `cland rule add <text> --scope <roles>|all --reason <text>`, `cland rule edit <id> [--text t] [--scope s] [--reason r]`, `cland rule retire <id> --reason <text>`, `cland rule list [--all] [--role r]` and `cland rule show <id>`, each with `--json`. The session tools `rule.add`, `rule.edit` and `rule.retire` take the same fields plus an origin, and every role may read with `rule.list`.
- **Who records a rule.** The write tools belong to the Coordinator and the Aide. A Coordinator's write names as its origin the human's message that stated the rule (its topic and message id), and the hub refuses one whose origin is not a message by the human, so the Coordinator never invents a rule. An Aide speaks for the human, so its rule names the Aide as its origin. Other roles propose a rule to the Coordinator in their item topic. The shell and the workbench record `shell` or `workbench` as the origin, and the seed records the memory file.
- **What the clause carries.** After the clause text, a section "Project rules for your role" lists each active rule in scope as `rule <n>: <text> (reason: <reason>)`, in id order; a role with none says so. The brief at launch ends with the same list, so a session reads the rules before its first action. Retired rules appear in neither.
- **How a change arrives.** A new, edited or retired rule is an event of the new kind `rule`. The hub delivers it to every running session whose role is in its scope, with no subscription needed, at the session's next turn (`digest: turn`), carrying the rule's full new text or its retirement. A session that missed it still gets the current rules in the clause the hub re-sends at a reconnect. It is never a needs-you, and the events view shows it.
- **The rulebook view.** `␣R`, free today, and the palette action "Rulebook" open the rulebook in the centre: one row per rule with its id, scope, status and date, active rules first and retired ones dimmed. Enter unfolds the text, the reason and the origin, and `gt` on an origin in a thread opens the topic at that message. `a` writes a new rule in a compose buffer (text, scope, reason) and records it on write, `e` edits the rule under the cursor, and `X` retires it with a reason.
- **Memories as caches.** The Coordinator's and the Aide's clauses say to record a rule with `rule.add` and never only in a harness memory; a memory that repeats a rule names its id.
- **The seed task.** One task under this epic, done by an Aide the Coordinator launches for it (crew.toml's `aide` policy is per item); the task names the memory folders to read. The Aide records each of the eight rules of §3.2 with `cland rule add`, with its scope, its reason and the memory file as its origin, adds to each migrated memory a line naming its rule id, and posts the list on the item. It records nothing beyond the eight: another rule found in the memories is listed on the item for the human.
- **The heartbeat setting.** `heartbeat` in `[crew.<role>]` takes a duration of at least one minute, or `"off"`. A Coordinator without the key gets `"1h"`, and any other role without it has none. `cland init` writes `heartbeat = "1h"` for the Coordinator, `cland crew show` lists it, `cland crew set coordinator.heartbeat 30m` sets it, and the next firing uses the new interval. Tests shorten it with an environment variable, as `CLAND_IDLE_NOTIFY_MS` shortens the idle threshold.
- **The clock.** Each session whose role has a heartbeat has its own schedule, counted from its launch. The next firing time is kept in `hub.db`, so a hub restart keeps the schedule, and a firing that fell due while the hub was down fires once after its start.
- **The digest.** The hub computes it at the firing, in two parts. In flight: the claimed items by status with their sessions, the running and queued runs, the open asks and the live leases. Stale, each row with its age: an item in `review` with no pending review request and no verdict at its head; an item `ready` and not merged; a session idle longer than `[inbox] idle_minutes`; a run past its timeout, or ended with no posted result; an ask open longer than the interval. An item or an ask counts as stale only after one full interval in that state. Each part lists at most ten rows and summarises the rest ("and 12 more"), as a digest does (v0.1 §3.9).
- **Delivery and coalescing.** A heartbeat is an event of the new kind `heartbeat` addressed to its session, not a subscription. On an idle session it starts a turn. On a busy session, or one waiting for approval, it waits as one entry of the next turn's digest, and a newer heartbeat replaces an undelivered older one. It never steers a running turn and is never a needs-you. The events view shows one row per firing, at the background layer, with the session and the counts; its kind filter takes `9` for `heartbeat`, and `rule`, the tenth kind, is filtered from the palette, which lists every kind.
- **The Coordinator on a heartbeat.** Its clause says: read the digest; repair what the Coordinator owns (request the missing review, merge a ready item through the gate, ask an idle session for its state, request a run that never reported again); escalate to the human with an ask only for a decision, a spend past a cap, or a stale row that survives two heartbeats after its repair; end a heartbeat with nothing stale without a message.
- **The relation.** `follows` is a list of epic ids in the item's frontmatter, beside `blocked_by`. `task create --follows <id>`, `task link <id> --follows <id>` and `--unfollow <id>`, and the same fields of the `task.link` tool set and remove it; any prefix resolves, and the hub refuses a cycle and an edge between items other than epics. `task view`, the card and the explorer show it beside the blockers.
- **When a follow is met.** A follow is met when its predecessor is closed, or when the predecessor has task children and all of them are closed, its last ticket merged. `task view` shows "follows E-<n>: met" or the tickets still open. Only `blocked_by` makes an item blocked in `task list` and the panels. The Coordinator's clause starts an epic when its blockers are closed and its follows are met.
- **The merge hold.** While a predecessor epic is open with its follow met and its demo pending, the merge gate holds a ticket of an epic that follows it when the ticket's diff touches a file that the predecessor's merges changed, read from the `Item:` trailers on `dev`. The refusal names the predecessor, its pending demo and the files, and the `merge` skill waits it out. A ticket with no overlap merges at once. The hold lifts when the predecessor's QA verdict is recorded, whatever its result.
- **Preparing the next epic.** The Coordinator's clause and the `to-tickets` and `plan-epic` skills say: when every ticket of an epic's last stage is in review, cut the following epic's tickets and write its plan, so that its first stage launches on the last merge.
- **The demo lease.** `cland demo start <epic> [--commit <sha>]` asks the hub for a droplet for the epic's demo: the hub acquires it under a lease within `remote_budget` and the daily cap, delivers the commit (the `dev` tip by default), and prepares it as for a suite run, Neovim included. `cland demo exec <epic> -- <command>` runs one command there as the ordinary user, in the delivered tree, and returns its output and exit code; a headless workbench (`cland --headless --qa`) runs the same way. `cland demo stop <epic>` releases the droplet, and the lease also ends at the epic's verdict or at its lifetime. The create, the destroy and the cost post on the epic. The `qa` skill's recorder runs each case through it, and cases that need macOS run locally at the same commit. When no remote slot or budget is left, `demo start` says so and QA runs the demo locally, with the hold still in force.
- **Fresh demo verdicts.** A demo's verdict names its commit. The hub accepts an epic verdict whose commit is on `dev` when the commits after it touch none of the epic's surfaces, and the `qa` skill's re-check of `dev` after the cases reads the same rule instead of reporting BLOCKED on any move.
- **The plan.** The rulebook, the heartbeat and the lane flow touch different code, so the plan may run them as parallel lanes; the seed waits for rules to reach sessions, and the demo lease waits for `follows`.

## Tracer-bullet order

1. **The heartbeat.** The `heartbeat` setting, the schedule in `hub.db`, the digest, the turn only on an idle session, the `heartbeat` event kind and its row in the events view, and the Coordinator's clause. Demo: in a scratch project with a fake Coordinator at `heartbeat = "1m"`, a planted review item with no request and an unanswered ask appear in the next heartbeat's digest, which starts a turn on the idle session; on a busy session the heartbeat folds into the next turn's digest, and the inbox count stays the same.
2. **`follows` and the merge hold.** The relation in the item file, the CLI and the tools; the follow met on the last merge; the hold at the gate; and the clause and skills that prepare the next epic during review. Demo: in a scratch project E2 follows E1; when E1's last ticket merges, `task view E2` shows the follow met; a ticket of E2 that touches a file E1 changed is held with a refusal naming E1's pending demo, another merges at once, and the held one merges after E1's verdict.
3. **The rulebook and `cland rule`.** The file, its parser and writer, the ids and origins, the commands, and the reload on change. Demo: `cland rule add` with a scope and a reason writes `## R-1` with its fields to `.cland/RULES.md`, `cland rule edit` and `cland rule retire` change it, and `cland rule list --all --json` reads both states.
4. **Rules reach sessions.** The rules in the clause and the brief, the `rule.*` tools with their origin rule, and the `rule` event to running sessions in scope. Demo: with a fake Coordinator and a fake Implementer, a rule scoped to `implementer` and recorded from the human's message reaches the Implementer at its next turn and in its clause after a reconnect, and not the Coordinator; a Coordinator's `rule.add` with no human origin is refused.
5. **The seed.** The Aide task records the eight rules with their origins and marks the memories. Demo: `cland rule list` on the live project shows the eight rules with their memory files as origins, and the Coordinator's next clause lists the ones in its scope.
6. **The rulebook in the workbench.** `␣R`, the rows, the origins, and adding, editing and retiring from the view. Demo: the headless workbench opens the rulebook with `␣R`, adds a rule with `a`, reads it in the list, and `gt` on a thread origin opens the topic at the human's message.
7. **Demos on a droplet.** `cland demo start`, `exec` and `stop`, the lease, the verdict's commit and the freshness rule, and the `qa` skill. Demo: QA starts a demo lease at the `dev` tip, runs a CLI case and a headless workbench case through `cland demo exec` while an unrelated commit lands on `dev`, and records a verdict the hub accepts; afterwards the droplet is gone and its cost is on the epic.

## Definition of done

QA runs the demo below on `dev`, playing the human's part through the `cland` CLI and a headless workbench (one `nvim --headless` process, keys by `nvim_input`, the screen read with `screenstring()`), on a droplet through the demo lease this epic adds, and records a clear verdict on this epic with each checkbox verified by its id; the epic then closes. The human does not run this demo (D16 and D19 of v0.1 §4).

In a scratch project with the fake harnesses, QA launches a fake Claude Code Coordinator and a fake Codex Implementer. A rule added from the shell with the scope `implementer` reaches the Implementer at its next turn and appears in its clause after a reconnect, and not in the Coordinator's; an edit and a retirement reach it the same way. The Coordinator's `rule.add` from the human's message records a rule with that origin, while one with no human origin and an Implementer's are refused. In the headless workbench QA opens the rulebook with `␣R`, reads each rule's scope, status and date, unfolds one to its reason and origin, follows a thread origin to the human's message, and adds a rule from the view. With `cland crew set coordinator.heartbeat 1m`, QA plants a review item with no request, a ready item, a session idle past `idle_minutes`, a run that never reported and an unanswered ask, and reads each in the next heartbeat's digest; with the Coordinator busy, the heartbeat folds into its next turn's digest; the inbox count does not change, and the events view shows the heartbeat rows under their kind. QA links two scratch epics with `--follows`, merges the first one's last ticket and reads the follow met; a ticket of the second that touches a file the first changed is held with a refusal naming the pending demo, another merges, and the held one merges after the first epic's verdict. The demo runs at a named `dev` commit, and a commit that lands on `dev` meanwhile on other files does not block the verdict. On the live project, `cland rule list` shows the eight seeded rules with their origins.

- [ ] C1. `.cland/RULES.md` holds one rule per heading with an id a plain number, a scope, the date, the reason, a status and an origin; `cland rule add`, `edit`, `retire`, `list` and `show` read and write it, and the `rule.add`, `rule.edit` and `rule.retire` tools do the same for the Coordinator, from a human message only, and for the Aide.

## Dogfooding

The build uses each part as soon as it merges. When the heartbeat slice merges and the hub restarts, the Coordinator runs with `heartbeat = "1h"`, and the hourly checks kept outside the hub stop. When `follows` merges, the Coordinator turns the two lane edges into follows ("OpenCode v2 hygiene" follows this epic, and "Hub hygiene" follows E-387), unlinking the `blocked_by` edges with `task link --unblock`, so that each lane's next epic starts on the last merge; the release epic keeps its blocking edges. The seed is recorded as soon as rules reach sessions; from then on every clause carries the rules, and the Coordinator records a rule the human states in a thread with `rule.add` instead of its memory. This epic's own demo, and every demo after it, runs on a droplet through the demo lease.

## Constraints

- **Standing rules.** Every artifact, item, commit and doc in English. Sub-agents never use the hub: the cland tools belong to the session that started them. Only `cland release` pushes to GitHub: commit on the task branch `t/<id>-<slug>` in its worktree, push it to `origin`, the local territory, and reach `dev` only through `cland merge` and its verdict gate. Suites run through `cland verify` (D25 and D29 of v0.1 §4). The hub's frame protocol is the first test seam (a real hub, a real spoke, the CLI against a temporary project; `hub/test/harness.ts`), the fake harnesses in `hub/test/fakes/` the second, with the Neovim UI headless from the protocol's other side; no new seams inside the hub. Items are written through `cland task` and the task tools, never as hand-written item files. The `opencode` CLI never runs inside a session until T-296 lands. The DigitalOcean token is never stored.
- **ADRs.** 0001 (Roles are hub-held state): the rules ride the clause the hub delivers. 0002 (Tracker files are the source of truth): the rulebook is a committed file of the project that the hub reads as it reads `roles.toml`, and `follows` lives in the item's frontmatter. 0007 (Events reach sessions as deliveries): a rule change and a heartbeat are events digested at turn boundaries, and neither steers a running turn.
- **Tests.** The heartbeat is driven through a short interval in tests. The demo lease is tested against E-271's fake DigitalOcean API and fake machine (`hub/test/fakes/digitalocean/`); a real droplet is QA's check, never part of `npm test`.
- **Risks.**
  - A heartbeat that wakes a busy crew is noise, which is why it never steers and folds into the next digest.
  - A long rulebook lengthens every clause, which is why a clause carries only the rules in its scope.
  - The hold could stall the next epic; it applies only to files the predecessor changed and lifts on the predecessor's verdict.
  - The demo lease shares `remote_budget` and the $3 daily cap with verification and E-387's sharded close runs, so a busy day sends a demo to the local machine.
  - Rule ids share the release prefix; the `rule <n>` form keeps them apart.
- **Size.** About eight sessions on the v0 scale.
- **Order.** First in the rules lane, with no blocker. "OpenCode v2 hygiene" follows it, and "Release v0.1.3 from the item" waits for the ends of both lanes.

## Goal

v0.1.2 "Working with items": the human works with items in cland as a full planning and tracking tool, not only watches status in the side panel. The core is the item explorer (T-243) with the human's item card (T-244), the release scope by epics (T-237, T-238), categories outside epics (T-245), id prefixes by kind (T-241) and done items distinct in the graph (T-242). Everything else is around that core.

## Notes

Scope by decision D21 (2026-10-11): everything from the v0.1.1 run that needed the human's decisions or design grilling. Grilled with the human on 2026-10-12 in three rounds (recorded above and in `docs/spec/v0.1.2.md` §3 and §4). Version 0.1.2 is the human's recorded version. The build ran in two lanes, hub and Neovim. "Test speed: quick wins" (E-386) joined the release on 2026-10-14, after D29 and the test-speed research Q-384. The crew was the same as in v0.1.1: Implementers on Codex gpt-6.1-sol, Claude Code roles on sonnet and a Reviewer pool of 2. The stand-in cland-impl answered for the human under D24. T-248 (the key-encoding matrix in the human's own terminals) moved to Tech debt and does not hold the release.

The goal: the human uses cland to plan and track items, and no longer only watches status in the side panel. The core is the item explorer and its card, the release scope by epics, categories outside epics, id prefixes by kind and done items shown distinctly.

What the human can now do, by epic:

- **E-268 Suite spend and Linux portability.** The suite runs on Linux as it does on macOS. On a c-8 DigitalOcean droplet, as an ordinary user, typecheck and the full suite are green: 1832 tests pass, and six platform skips each name a reason (A-2028). A spawn census (`node hub/test/spawn-census.mjs run`) shows where the suite's processes come from. The big sources are cut: teardown by process group, a prepared fixture repository and a process listing that works on both platforms. QA clear: qa-2026-10-13-27-6 (A-2031).
- **E-269 Prefixes and categories.** An id shows its item's kind: `R-` release, `E-` epic, `T-` task, `Q-` question, `M-` map, `S-` spec, `C-` category. All kinds share one counter, and any prefix with the right number still finds the item, so old `T-` ids keep working. The live tracker migrated on 2026-10-13. Tech debt (C-216), Bugs (C-325), Follow-ups (C-326) and Ideas (C-327) are root containers beside the releases. Agents file finds into them with `--parent C-n`, and the Coordinator takes their work when the release has nothing unblocked (`idle_from`). The items panel ends with a count line for the categories. QA clear: qa-2026-10-13-27-4.
- **E-270 Status, fields and instrumentation.** `planned` now comes from the epic plan: the items of the current stage are planned, and the hub moves the next stage when one completes. The release scope shows only the release's own items, and everything else is under the `all` filter. The card gets its fields without a request per row: the closing time, verified/total and the latest verify result. The journal now records session usage. Tasks carry a required `size`, an optional `regression_of`, the model of every launch and the verdict scope, so models can be compared within size classes. QA clear: qa-2026-10-13-27-8 (A-2074).
- **E-271 Remote executors.** `cland verify` runs a suite on a DigitalOcean droplet through cland's own executor interface. The executor is chosen per run (`--executor local|droplet`), with a per-project default under `[verification]`, and there is no silent fallback. The local machine stays one executor with a cap of one. The hub enforces the remote budget, the lifetime, the run timeout and a daily cap (defaults 4, 110 min, 75 min and $5 a day; this project ran on 2, 60 min, 50 min and $3 a day). It also runs a watchdog and sweeps droplets by the `cland` tag. Spend is kept in a host-wide ledger, `~/.cland/executor/spend.json`. The token stays in the human's shell and is never stored. A c-16 run took 1057 s on the hub phase for $0.16: about 25% faster than a c-8, at about 1.7 times the cost. QA clear: qa-2026-10-14-27-9.
- **E-272 Accounts and limits.** Accounts are named in `~/.config/cland/accounts.toml` (names and paths only, never a secret). `roles.toml` and launches pin a session to an account by name. The sessions panel opens with an accounts block: each window the harness reports (5-hour, weekly), its used share and its reset time. A limited account is highlighted and refuses new launches, and the human picks another; cland never rotates accounts or fails over. The Claude adapter polls `claude agents --json` at most once per 30 s per config directory, and a signed-out directory raises one event and one message (T-265). QA clear: qa-2026-10-14-27-11 (A-2531).
- **E-274 Inbox and the events view.** The inbox holds only what needs the human now, in four sections. Asks and approvals come first, then plan approvals. Requests to the human use the new `request` kind: a review, a QA or a handover. Messages come last. Each row leaves by its own rule, and the chip shows the inbox count. Everything else is in the events view (`␣E`): newest first, grouped by day, 200 rows at a time, with `A` to load older rows and `gM` to mute a subject. The old notification list with `d`/`D` is gone. QA clear: qa-2026-10-13-27-2 (A-1673), after a first run failed on a duplicate warning row (T-310, fixed).
- **E-275 Sessions: stopped sessions, verifiers' items, the queue line.** `r` resumes a stopped session through the harness's own resume and keeps its name, role and claim. `d` archives a session. A stopped crew session archives itself one hour after its item merges or closes, or otherwise 24 hours after it stops; Aides never archive themselves. `cland session prune --older-than` deletes old records. A verifier's row shows its latest hold and `+N`, and a pending request shows dimmed. The `verify:` line summarises the queue and opens the queue view. The human's `npm test` goes through the same queue unless `--force` is given. QA clear: qa-2026-10-13-27-3 (A-1820).
- **E-276 The explorer and the card.** `␣e` (also the startup view) opens an outline tree in the centre. The root is the current release with its epics and tasks, and folded roots hold the categories, the unscheduled items and the other releases. The card of the row under the cursor sits beside the tree, with the summary and the facts first and the agents' text folded. Rows show done/total, status bars, the stage and the lead. Done items follow the live ones in the done colour, and `D` hides them. `s` rescopes the tree, with breadcrumbs. The explorer edits nothing: `m` and `M` send the Coordinator a message about an item or a selection, and `M` sends it in the item's own topic. At release scope the side panel shows epics as folded rows. Done items stay readable in the graph, the panel and the board. The plan was approved by the stand-in under D24. QA clear: qa-2026-10-14-27-10.
- **E-386 Test speed: quick wins.** A task run now verifies what its diff selects, under wider package rules. Replayed on the last 40 merges, the selection goes from full 37 / hub-only 2 / Neovim-only 1 to 26 / 9 / 5. A Neovim-only run took 112 s, against about 15 minutes before. Fake harnesses default to fast turns, and timer-bound tests run on schedules set through the environment (T-389: −26% over the harness files, measured under load). `hub/test/durations.json` sets a budget: a new test over 5 s or a new file over 60 s fails the run, and a known one that slows down is reported as a `duration regression`. `cland` loads only the subcommand it runs: `--help` loads 2 `hub/src` modules, and its median fell from 186 to 84 ms under load. Fixture hubs skip the start-up orphan sweep, and teardown signals only the processes the test recorded. Inspection spawns in default-subscriptions fell by about 63%, and a partial full-run census counted 23,476 against 29,203. QA (qa-2026-10-15-27-12, A-2738) measured 1171 s less common hub test-time and a full run 230 s shorter (919 s against 1149 s), against the before run A-2450 and the after run A-2714. The census is a lower bound of 23,684 inspection spawns at 22.6 per daemon start; the full targets move to T-448, and the under-5 s timer target to T-443.
- **E-273 Release v0.1.2 from the item.** If a tracker storage operation stalls while the hub serves, the hub logs it, tells the sessions and the workbench, and exits non-zero. No mutation admitted after the stall commits, and `hub/README.md` describes the restart (T-253). A cancelled suite attempt no longer supersedes green cache evidence for its tree, while a failed one still does (T-254). T-253 merged as a30df82c and T-254 as 8b2a3d7a.

Decisions of the run:

- **D23 accepted (v0.1.2 §4).** The tracker-stall detection and the bounded stop from v0.1.1 stay as shipped. The serving-time fail-fast exit is T-253, ordinary tech debt, and it ships in this release.
- **D24 (2026-10-12).** The stand-in cland-impl answers every ask on the human's behalf, including the explorer plan approval.
- **D25 (2026-10-13).** Review first: `cland verify` runs only after a clear review, at the exact reviewed head. Droplets serve as a second Linux slot, with the `cland` tag, at most 30 minutes of life (45 for c-8 acceptance runs), one at a time and at most $2 a day.
- **D26** is reserved for T-282's narrowing fallback; no use of it is recorded.
- **D27 (2026-10-13).** E-271 ships the remote budget, lifetime, run timeout and daily cap as config that the hub enforces (defaults 4 / 110 min / 75 min / $5; this project 2 / 60 min / 50 min / $3). c-8 is the default size, and one c-16 run measured the speed. No phase split this release.
- **D28 (2026-10-14).** The project switched its verification to droplets (`executor = "droplet"`, `remote_budget = 2`) after T-347 merged. The release's final local run covers the macOS-only cases.
- **D29 (2026-10-14).** A task verifies only what its diff selects, plus the test files it touched, and never `verify all` by default. Full suites run on integrated `dev`: per batch of about three merges, at each stage and epic close, and before the release.
- **Lane flow (stand-in, 2026-10-13).** The edges between consecutive epics in a lane were removed. The next epic starts once the previous one's code is merged, and its merges wait for the previous epic's QA verdict.
- **Local task gates (human, ask de65131f, 2026-10-14).** Tasks verify locally on the Mac until the shared Linux fixes (T-429, T-430) merge. The Reviewer judges the same head's local run in place of a red droplet run.
- **Duration budget (human, ask 225afa4b, 2026-10-15).** The budget fails a run only for a test or file new to the manifest. A known one over budget reports a `duration regression` line and does not fail the run.
